The information for the Prime Visa has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The Capital One Venture Rewards is a great option for those who want to earn flexible rewards without worrying about different spending category bonuses. The Venture Rewards earns 2 miles per dollar spent on all purchases — ensuring that you earn bonus miles no matter if you’re buying stocking stuffers or perusing Cyber Monday deals.

There’s also flexibility in how you redeem those miles you earn. You can use your miles to “pay” yourself back for travel booked in the past 90 days. Or, you can transfer your miles to 15-plus airline and hotel loyalty programs to book new travel. You can also redeem miles for gift cards or statement credits for eligible purchases.

To learn more, read our full review of the Venture Rewards.

Learn more: Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card

The is a great option for earning bonus rewards year-round, thanks to its rotating quarterly categories.

For the fourth quarter of 2026, cardholders can earn 5% cash back on grocery store purchases and American Red Cross donations, plus an elevated 7% cash back on dining purchases. That could come in handy if you're stocking up for holiday gatherings or dining out with family and friends.

These bonus rates apply to up to $1,500 in combined purchases across the quarterly categories through Dec. 31, after which you'll earn 1% back. You must activate the categories by Dec. 14 to qualify.

While 5% cash back is appealing on its own, the Freedom Flex can be even more valuable when paired with a Chase card that earns transferable Ultimate Rewards points, such as the (see rates and fees), or the (see rates and fees).

By combining your rewards, you can transfer points to airline and hotel partners, including United MileagePlus and World of Hyatt, potentially getting more value from your holiday spending. Note that the Sapphire Preferred offers a 4:3 transfer ratio for World of Hyatt.

To learn more, read our full review of the Freedom Flex.

If you’re a regular Amazon shopper, the Prime Visa is the card for you, with no annual fee (though it requires an Amazon Prime membership).

With Black Friday and Cyber Monday coming, you want a card that gives you the biggest bang for your holiday shopping buck. The Prime Visa offers unlimited 5% on Amazon, Whole Foods and Chase Travel, 2% on restaurants, gas stations and local transit and commuting and 1% on all other purchases. Additionally, earn 10% or more on a rotating selection of items and categories on Amazon.com.

If you don’t have the card already, new applicants will instantly get a $150 Amazon gift card upon approval, exclusively for Prime members.

To learn more, check out our full review of the Prime Visa.

Without question, the is one of the best cards for foodies. The card offers an impressive 4 points per dollar spent at U.S. supermarkets (up to $25,000 spent per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent) and restaurants worldwide (on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

While the earning rate for nonbonus purchases yields 1 point per dollar spent, you may want to consider paying with the Amex Gold this holiday season for its strong purchase protection policy. Eligible items are covered for up to $10,000 in theft, damage, or loss within the first 90 days of purchase (up to $50,000 per calendar year).*

That’s considerable, especially if you buy big-ticket items like electronics or furniture.

The Amex Gold also comes with extended warranty protection, which prolongs a U.S. manufacturer’s warranty by an additional year on eligible warranties of five years or less.*

You’ll never know when you need to rely on these protections, but they can be quite valuable and may be worth sacrificing the bonus points you’d earn from the other cards on this list, even after factoring in the $325 annual fee.

*Eligibility and benefit levels vary by card. Terms, conditions, and limitations apply. Visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for details. Policies are underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Gold.

If you have the ability to park a significant amount of your investments and savings at Bank of America or Merrill, the is a great option for holiday purchases.

While the card comes with reasonable (though not earth-shattering) earning rates of 2 points per dollar spent on travel and dining and 1.5 points per dollar spent on all purchases (which can be redeemed at the rate of 1 cent per point), the real value of this card comes when you can make it to either the Preferred Honors or Premier award tiers in the BofA Rewards™ program.

By doing so, the everyday earning rate on this card can jump all the way up to roughly 2.6 points for every dollar spent, making it a terrific choice for holiday gifts.

To learn more, read our full review of the Bank of America Premium Rewards.

The final card on our list earns a spot in part for its simplicity. The offers a flat 1% back on every purchase plus another 1% back as you pay your bill (up to a 2% total return).

While this return rate on everyday purchases doesn’t compare to the potential returns highlighted above, this is automatic; it results in cold, hard cash in your account. For many shoppers, a no-annual-fee card like this fits the bill.

To learn more, read our full review of the Double Cash.

Holiday spending can do more than check gifts off your list — it can also help you reach big credit card goals. If you’ve recently opened a new card, consider putting your holiday purchases toward the minimum spending requirement to earn a valuable welcome bonus. Just be sure to budget responsibly and pay off your balance in full as often as you can.

If you already have multiple cards, check whether any offer calendar-year spending bonuses or perks that reset soon. Concentrating your purchases on one card could help you unlock statement credits, free nights or elite status before the year ends.

Another easy way to earn extra rewards is through online shopping portals. These portals let you earn additional points, miles or cash back just by clicking through before you buy (no special credit card required).

To find the best offer, use CashBack Monitor, which compares earning rates across dozens of portals for the same retailer. You can also install your preferred portal’s browser extension, so you’ll never miss out on bonus rewards during checkout.

Related: The best credit card welcome bonuses of the month

The holiday season doesn’t have to drain your wallet, and with the right credit card strategy, your spending can actually pay you back. Focus on cards that match your shopping habits, whether that means flat-rate cash back, bonus rewards on popular retailers or flexible travel points you can redeem later.

Pair your card with online shopping portals and seasonal category bonuses to earn even more rewards on every purchase. And if you’re opening a new card, use your holiday spending to hit minimum spend requirements and unlock valuable welcome offers.

With a little planning, your holiday shopping can turn into a rewards windfall, from extra points and cash back to future flights, hotel stays or statement credits, making this season both festive and rewarding.

#6096. FAA Projects Busiest Thanksgiving Travel Week in 16 Years

More than 417,000 flights will operate in the U.S. this week and early next week as Americans travel ahead of and after Thanksgiving, according to the FAA.

If accurate, that figure would translate to the busiest Thanksgiving travel period in 16 years.

Tuesday is expected to be the single busiest day of the interval, with more than 52,000 flights.

Air traffic will dip only slightly on Wednesday (49,831 flights) and nearly halve on Thanksgiving Day (27,619 flights) itself, the FAA said, with a rebound following Friday to Tuesday, Dec. 1. There will be over 50,000 flights per day on the Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday after Thanksgiving.

Perhaps aiming to assuage concerns from the public after a turbulent couple of weeks, transportation officials said they are prioritizing traveler safety and taking “unprecedented action” to limit flight delays and cancellations.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy noted that the Trump administration has assembled a “tiger team” of experts to prevent another mass ground stop.

“Our air traffic controllers and safety professionals are working around the clock to keep Americans moving during what is expected to be the busiest Thanksgiving travel week in 16 years,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said in a statement. “The growing demand for air travel makes it more important than ever to continue modernizing our air traffic control system and build a national airspace system for the 21st century.”

The FAA is also advising travelers to get to the airport early and check with their airline for updates if bad weather seems likely to impact their trip. The agency noted the high likelihood of thunderstorms in the Southeast, Mid-Atlantic, and Northeast this week.

#6095. Delta Air Lines Set To Reveal New 17-Hour Nonstop Route Next Week: See Map Now

Delta Air Lines has fallen behind United Airlines in terms of its transpacific network in recent years, but the Atlanta-based carrier has started to close that gap. This year, it reinstated flights between Los Angeles and Hong Kong, and next year it is reinstating its nonstop services between Seattle and Tokyo Narita, and also launching flights to Manila.

The airline is now preparing to announce yet another addition to its network next week. The SkyTeam member is hosting a major event in Seattle on December 2, where it is set to unveil at least one new route. It is widely expected to be Singapore, which it last served in 2019 via Tokyo Narita International Airport (NRT).

Delta has been planning a return to the Lion City for some time. As Simple Flying reported in August, the airline's Chief Commercial Officer, Joe Esposito, confirmed that Singapore Changi Airport (SIN) was part of its future network plans. There has since been further evidence that the service could launch as early as next year.

Evidently, according to View From The Wing, the Atlanta-based airline identified Singapore as one of its new markets for 2027 in a July 29 presentation to a Pacific air traffic coordination group. The airline stated in the presentation, “New markets announced for 2027 are Manila and Singapore.”

The service is expected to operate from the airline's West Coast hub at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) and would have an estimated block time of around 17 hours. Delta will likely deploy its Airbus A350-900 on the route, although the larger A350-1000 could eventually take over the service.

Based on what is known so far, the service could launch in the summer or fall of 2027. Delta previously indicated that its Singapore service would follow the launch of its Los Angeles–Manila route. The latter is scheduled to commence on March 28, 2027, initially operating three times weekly before increasing to daily on June 7.

Singapore was once part of an extensive connecting network through Tokyo that Delta inherited from Northwest Airlines. When the carrier decided to withdraw from the Singapore market, it cited financial pressure on the route. Growing nonstop capacity between the US and Singapore, stronger brand loyalty towards local carriers, and competition from Star Alliance members at Changi made it increasingly difficult for Delta to compete.

But the proposed service would put Delta in direct competition with Singapore Airlines. According to scheduled data from aviation analytics provider Cirium, the Singaporean flag carrier operates five weekly flights between Seattle and Singapore. It also dominates the wider US–Singapore market, as noted above in the table. Meanwhile, United Airlines is currently the only US carrier serving Singapore nonstop, operating twice daily from San Francisco.

Only 2 airports in the Pacific are in Delta Air Lines' plans. Is this really enough, or is this actually a global trend in development?

It is interesting to see Delta expanding its presence in Asia. Its overall capacity in Asia is up around 5.8% this year compared to 2025. As noted earlier, there have been several interesting developments in its transpacific network. In June, the airline reinstated daily flights between its Southern California hub and Hong Kong International Airport (HKG) after decades of absence on the route.

Notably, it also marked its return to Hong Kong for the first time since 2018. From March 27, 2027, the airline will resume daily flights between Seattle and Tokyo Narita for the first time since March 2020, complementing its existing service to Tokyo Haneda Airport (HND). Elsewhere, it will make its debut in the Philippines market.

While not part of its regular network, the SkyTeam member has also scheduled a handful of nonstop flights to and from Las Vegas Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) for the upcoming Consumer Electronics Show (CES). These include flights between Las Vegas and Hong Kong on January 4 and 10, and between Las Vegas and Taipei on January 5 and 10.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

We don't know for sure what the big announcement will be at next week's event but you may well be correct: SEA-SIN makes a certain amount of sense. They definitely want to return to the Singapore market and SEA is their best positioned hub from which to do so, especially considering the Delta fleet's maximum range capabilities. I wish them well but SQ could well respond by increasing their schedule from SEA ro daily. The D1 lounge at SEA is very nice but the advantage will be SQ's at Changi--and I suspect SQ will have an edge in onboard service, especially in economy class. I don't know how much feed SQ gets at SEA, given that Star Alliance and UA don't have much presence here and SQ and AS no longer really partner, but their existing SEA-SIN service seems to be doing OK. DL may be more dependent on feed at SEA than SQ but it has a strong route network at SEA. In DL's battle with AS, opening a SIN route may also serve to keep AS off of that route, especially given SQ's presence. I am definitely interested in DL's announcement next week.

Well good luck Delta Airlines returning to this area, can bet Singapore Airlines flies from Vancouver Inter'l Airport as well so this might make things challenging if this is the case - otherwise I would take either Cathay Pacific (via Hong Kong) or Philippine Airlines (via Manila ) or San Francisco / Los Angles to reach Singapore !!

#6093. WestJet Quietly Cancels 3 International Routes: See Full List Now

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Canada's second-largest airline will quietly pull out of Tulum. The airport, which serves the Southern Riviera Maya, will lose another airline despite strong travelers' interest in the region. Many carriers have scaled back operations at the airport, focusing instead on the region's primary gateway, Cancun. United Airlines was the latest major airline to announce it would terminate operations at the airport.

WestJet's withdrawal from Tulum will leave just two other Canadian airlines serving the airport, with Air Canada maintaining flights from Montreal and Toronto while Air Transat continues serving Tulum from Montreal and Quebec City.

On January 9, Montreal will lose its WestJet link to Tulum, as the airline terminates its Boeing 737 MAX 8 service to the Mexican airport. WestJet currently operates the route up to three times a week, with the link being operated for the carrier's package holiday subsidiary, Sunwing Vacations.

Mexico in general, and especially Cancun and the Riviera Maya, continues to be a popular year-round destination for Canadians looking for vacations to the south. WestJet's decision to drop its services to Tulum raises questions about the route's load factors, as the airline abruptly stopped flying there in the middle of the Canadian winter, usually a popular time to travel south.

With WestJet removing its flights from Montreal to Tulum, it leaves just Air Canada and Air Transat operating the service nonstop to Tulum. From Montreal to Cancun, Air Canada, Air Canada Rouge, Flair Airlines, Air Transat and WestJet all maintain services either seasonally or year-round.

Montréal-Pierre Elliott Trudeau International Airport (YUL)

Canada's largest city will also lose its WestJet link to Tulum, as on January 9 the carrier will axe its service to the Southern Riviera Maya airport. This will leave Air Canada as the sole operator on the city pair, making it yet another carrier unable to make operations at Tulum viable.

Instead, flights to and from the state of Quintana Roo will now be focused on Cancun, where WestJet maintains year-round flights. From Cancun, Toronto is served by Air Canada, Air Canada Rouge, Air Transat, Flair, Porter Airlines, and WestJet.

Toronto Pearson International Airport (YYZ)

WestJet, up until January served Tulum seasonally and has not maintained a year-round service. The same is true for Air Canada and Air Transat.

Three are long-haul, while the rest are within the Caribbean, Mexico and the US. Find them all here!

WestJet's home at Calgary is the third and final Tulum route the airline has cut. WestJet maintains a seasonal service to Tulum, flying up to twice weekly with a mix of the 737-800 and MAX 8. On January 14, the service to the Mexican tourist destination will be shelved, leaving no flights to Canada's west.

Despite Tulum continuing to be a world-class tourist destination, the local airport has struggled to gain momentum since its opening. WestJet joins a long list of airlines that have opted to withdraw service to the airport in recent months, most recently United Airlines, which will terminate its routes from Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) on January 2 and George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) on January 4. Domestic carrier Volaris will also end its nonstop flights to Tulum from Guadalajara on January 7.

Remaining airlines serving Tulum after January will be Air Canada and Air Transat from Canada, and American Airlines and Delta Air Lines with services to the US, as well as Mexicana de Aviación and Viva with domestic services within Mexico.

#6091. Atmos For Business: Earn Up To 23.5x Points On Alaska & Hawaiian Flights

Atmos for Business is the small business rewards program of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines, and it runs parallel to the Atmos Rewards program (Atmos for Business used to be known as the EasyBiz program).

Most major US airlines have a small business rewards program, and the intent is to offer extra rewards when businesses book travel. The good news is that even small businesses qualify for this, and it can really boost the rewards you earn.

Along those lines, in light of the recent refresh of the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card (learn more), I think this program is worth a close look. Long story short, Atmos Rewards members could be earning up to 23.5x points per dollar spent on airfare. Based on my valuation of 1.5 cents per Atmos Rewards point, that’s the equivalent of a jaw dropping 35.25% return on eligible spending. That’s simply unrivaled.

Atmos for Business is the self-managed business travel program by Alaska and Hawaiian, intended for small and medium sized businesses.

The program is open to companies and organizations with at least $5,000 in annual travel spending, so if you’re a frequent flyer with the company and have a small business, that’s not much of a hurdle. You can add an unlimited number of employees to your account, and all of their spending counts toward that requirement.

Now, the terms suggest that you must have spent at least $5,000 or more on eligible Alaska and Hawaiian travel in the last 15 months, though in practice, that’s not directly enforced, best I can tell. After all, this is even intended to attract new businesses that may be looking to switch travel to Alaska or Hawaiian.

When a business enrolls in Atmos for Business, it’s assigned a company Atmos Rewards loyalty number. Atmos for Business then offers an impressive number of bonus rewards:

Beyond increased loyalty benefits for the business, Atmos for Business offers a platform that is supposed to make booking easier, with features like the following:

The total number of points that you can earn per dollar spent with Atmos for Business is pretty incredible, assuming you have the Atmos Rewards Business Card. As of 2027, Atmos Rewards members can choose how they get rewarded for flying, and they can choose to earn rewards based on distance flown, dollars spent, or segments flown.

Assuming you choose to earn based on how much you spend, here’s how the math works out:

As you can see, a non-elite member booking through the Atmos for Business portal and paying with the Atmos Rewards Business Card would earn 15x points per dollar spent, while a Titanium member booking through the Atmos for Business portal and paying with the Atmos Rewards Business Card would earn 22.5x points.

This doesn’t factor in the extra 1x points that the company earns, for a total of up to 23.5x points per dollar spent. Furthermore, it doesn’t factor in the 10% status points bonus, but that’s a different story.

While I’m going for top tier Atmos Rewards Titanium status, I still don’t fly with Alaska or Hawaiian often, given that I live in Miami, so it’s not the most practical carrier. Still, my goodness, the return on airfare spending is absolutely unreal here, if you are a loyalist.

To make sure there wasn’t any catch to all of this, I signed up for the Atmos for Business program. This was super straightforward — I just had to log into my Atmos Rewards account, and then fill out some basic company details.

This included the country my business is registered in, my business name, my tax ID, my phone number, and my address.

It was that easy, and I was registered instantly. The Atmos for Business program account management page looked mighty familiar, as it’s basically the same concept as the American AAdvantage Business program. There you can add travelers, manage payments, etc.

To actually book travel, you just select the “Book Travel” heading. That will bring you to a search that looks identical to what you’ll find on Alaska’s website, but it’s customized to Atmos for Business.

Pricing is identical to what you’d find directly on the websites of Alaska or Hawaiian, so that’s pretty tough to beat.

Atmos for Business is the small business rewards program of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. Even small businesses qualify, though the idea is that it’s for those who spend at least $5,000 per year on flights with the company across employees, which isn’t a very high bar.

The main advantage of Atmos for Business is that you earn one extra point per dollar spent, plus 10% bonus status points. But the area where the program gets really rewarding is if you have the Atmos Rewards Business Card, as that offers 10x points per dollar spent through Atmos for Business.

If you were an Atmos Rewards Titanium member booking through Atmos for Business and paying with the Atmos Rewards Business Card, you’d potentially earn a total of 23.5x points per dollar spent on airfare, with no caps. This is simply an amazing rate of return. Man, I’m really bummed that I can’t fly with Alaska or Hawaiian more, as that return on spending is something to get excited about.

What do you make of the Atmos for Business program?

#6090. Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

The new office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

Britt, R-Ala., said the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

“This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting new technologies and gaps between sectors,” she said in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”

The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide said.

The office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

The House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

Senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring

It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

“If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

#6089. Awful: American Dies After Picking Fight With MMA Fighter At Bangkok Hotel

An American who was reportedly yelling at staff at a hotel in Thailand ended up picking a fight with the wrong guest, and it ended up costing him his life. This is both tragic and insanely irresponsible on both sides… I just don’t get what people are thinking sometimes…

Media in Thailand is reporting on an incident that happened early this morning (Sunday, November 22, 2026), whereby a 46-year-old American tourist died at a hotel in Bangkok’s Phra Khanong area, after an altercation with a 39-year-old Italian man, who was reportedly an MMA fighter.

According to the initial police report, the American had been arguing loudly with the hotel staff at the reception desk, for reasons that are unclear as of now. As an Italian hotel guest walked past him and attempted to enter an elevator, the American reportedly grabbed him and pulled him out.

The confrontation escalated, and turned into a physical struggle, during which the Italian man placed the American man in a chokehold, until he lost consciousness. Hotel staff called emergency services, and while first responders performed CPR, the American couldn’t be revived. Police also found an abrasion on the victim’s forehead.

The Italian man remained at the scene, and told authorities that he had been acting in self-defense, after being attacked. Police took him into custody, and he potentially faces manslaughter charges, though the case is still being investigated.

The hotel at which this incident happened hasn’t yet been named, but this occurred at Sukhumvit Soi 48 — there are several hotels in that area, with the biggest “brand name” property being a Ramada Plaza by Wyndham.

I feel horribly for the family of the person who lost his life. I would have to imagine that odds are high that there were likely some substances involved here, and that this all happened after a big Saturday night out. After all, most people aren’t looking to get into a massive fight while getting their first cup of coffee in the morning (or maybe it’s just me?).

But my gosh, the “victim” here sounds like he was acting absolutely horribly, arguing with hotel staff, and then picking a fight with a random person. At the same time, that also doesn’t justify the response of getting into a conflict that leads to a fatality.

I absolutely love Thailand — the people are so friendly, the food is amazing, and the country also offers such diversity in terms of landscape, whether you want a city, a jungle, or a beach. However, there’s also no denying that the country (and particularly Bangkok) attracts a large percentage of tourists who are looking for debauchery.

None of this has anything to do with a conflict that gets to the point of costing someone their life, but I can’t help but mention that when I review hotels, I tend to take a lot of pictures in lobbies around 4-5AM, when it’s the emptiest (since I’m a morning person anyway). Virtually everywhere else in the world, there’s not a single soul awake in public. Bangkok is probably the one exception, where you see a countless number of people moving through lobbies, elevators, etc., engaged in various forms of “business.”

An American man lost his life in Bangkok early on Sunday morning, after picking a fight with the wrong person. The 46-year-old was reportedly shouting at hotel staff, and then attacked a 39-year-old Italian guest getting into the elevator unprovoked. That Italian man was reportedly an MMA fighter, who put him in a chokehold, to the point that the American lost his life. While the man claims he was acting in self defense, he now potentially faces manslaughter charges.

It’s really sad how people act sometimes. We only have one life to live, and how unfortunate to cut your life short so unnecessarily.

#6088. What Are The World’s Tallest & Highest Hotels? The Answer Is Tricky…

There’s something I really love about staying in a hotel room on a really high floor, where you’re so high up that you almost feel like you’re in an airplane. So, what are the tallest and highest hotels in the world? I want to talk about that in this post, and also discuss why the answer isn’t that straightforward.

The question of which hotel is the tallest and highest isn’t as straightforward as you might assume. And even once we do define it, there’s the question of the extent to which the answer is actually useful. First let’s cover the distinction between the tallest hotel and the highest hotel.

Generally speaking, the tallest hotel would be defined as the tallest building where a large percent of the structure is made up of the hotel. Most commonly, I see people suggest that this would include situations where at least 80% of the building is the hotel.

This is different than the highest hotel, which would be the hotel that is highest above the ground, even if it only takes up a small percentage of a mixed-use building, where there might be apartments, residences, etc.

In other words, a 50-story building that consists exclusively of a hotel would fall into the former category, while a 110-story building where the top 10 floors are a hotel would fall into the latter category.

With that out of the way, let’s talk about the properties that are remarkable in these categories…

First, let’s cover some of the world’s tallest hotels. We’ll define this as hotels where at least 80% of the building consists of the hotel facility.

Let me of course mention one downside of very tall standalone hotels — you could end up being on a very low floor. After all, if a high-rise consists exclusively (or almost exclusively) of hotel facilities, some people will end up on very low floors. The other downside, of course, is that these hotels are necessarily huge. If you prefer boutique hotels, you won’t find any on this list.

Currently, the tallest hotel in the world is Ciel Tower Dubai. The 1,042-room hotel opened in 2024, rises to a height of 1,227 feet (374 meters), and has 82 floors.

To go over the list of the top five tallest hotels in the world:

As you can see, it’s interesting (but perhaps not surprising) that all four of the world’s tallest hotels are in Dubai.

The Conrad Shanghai, meanwhile, is located in the Shimao International Plaza, and this is the perfect example of how it’s tough to define what is technically the tallest. While the building it’s in rises to such a high height, roughly 25% of that height is the spire. So technically it’s a very tall building, but the usable space isn’t as high as you’d assume.

If you ask me, the world’s highest hotels are much more interesting than the world’s tallest hotels. That’s because the world’s highest hotels typically take up the top floors of some gravity-defying skyscrapers, and therefore, they can also be boutique properties.

When defining the world’s tallest hotels, there are some general challenges:

Because of the above, there are some minor disagreements as to which hotel wins the title, but I’ll share my take (while acknowledging that I don’t have the ability to scale buildings with a measuring tape).

Currently, the highest hotel is the Rosewood Guangzhou. The 251-room hotel opened in 2019, and it’s located at the top of the CTF Finance Centre Guangzhou, which reaches a height of 1,739 feet (530 meters).

To go over the list of the top five highest hotels in the world:

As you can see, those last two properties are kind of hard to judge, and particularly J Hotel Shanghai is tricky, given that the property is split between different parts of the building.

As the inverse of the above, I should mention that the Armani Hotel Dubai is located within the Burj Khalifa, which is the world’s tallest building. However, it’s located at the very bottom of the building, so that’s hardly that useful, for these purposes, since the hotel only goes as high as 39 floors.

Lastly, in the interest of being thorough, if we’re going to define a hotel as being “highest” based on the altitude above sea level, then we’d of course end up with a completely different list. Hotel Tayka del Desierto is located near the Salar de Uyuni salt flats in Bolivia. It’s at an altitude of 14,800 feet (4,500 meters), so it’s generally considered to be the highest up hotel in the world.

I suppose depending on how we want to define “hotel,” there would probably be some simple guest houses at Everest Base Camp that go even higher, but I don’t think that’s within the spirit of what I’m trying to cover here.

If you ask me, it’s always fun to stay in a hotel room that’s really high up. There’s an important distinction between the tallest hotels and the highest hotels, though sometimes, the exact rankings are a bit blurred.

While I’ve long been interested in this, I enjoyed researching this a bit more closely, and actually having a (sort of) definitive list. Ciel Tower Dubai is the world’s tallest hotel, while the Rosewood Guangzhou is the world’s highest hotel (unless you want to consider the 120th floor of the J Hotel Shanghai separately from the rest of the property).

Have you stayed at any of the world’s tallest or highest hotels? Does it even hold any appeal to you?

#6087. FAA Bans Line Up And Wait Operations “Forever,” With Even More Delays Expected

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has introduced stricter requirements for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) operations at airports across the United States, effective November 24, 2026. The new rules require a dedicated air traffic control supervisor to oversee these operations, potentially preventing controllers at understaffed facilities from using the procedure. The change comes just as millions of Americans prepare to travel for Thanksgiving, raising concerns about longer departure queues and additional flight delays.

Despite reports describing the measure as a permanent nationwide ban, the FAA has not prohibited Line Up and Wait operations altogether. Instead, it has made them conditional on additional staffing, introducing another operational challenge for an air traffic control system already struggling with personnel shortages.

The new requirement is outlined in FAA Notice JO 7210.979, which mandates that a standalone watch supervision position must be staffed whenever Line Up and Wait operations are conducted. Previously, the relevant guidance recommended that the local control position should not be combined with other responsibilities. The updated wording makes this a mandatory requirement, meaning supervisors can no longer simultaneously perform other operational duties while overseeing these operations.

Line Up and Wait is a widely used air traffic control procedure that allows aircraft to enter an assigned runway and hold in position while waiting for takeoff clearance. It helps improve runway efficiency because departing aircraft are already positioned when the runway becomes available. However, under the new requirements, airports without sufficient personnel to provide dedicated supervision will have to keep aircraft waiting at taxiway holding points instead. This could reduce departure capacity, particularly during busy periods.

The timing is concerning because November 24 coincides with the beginning of one of America's busiest Thanksgiving travel periods. According to the FAA forecast reported by Traveling for Business, more than 52,000 flights were scheduled for that Tuesday, with over 417,000 expected throughout the nine-day holiday period.

FAA provided a statement to Simple Flying to clarify the new rule:

The FAA is taking proactive steps to further strengthen runway safety by enhancing staffing and supervisory requirements for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) at airports nationwide, effective Nov. 24, 2026. These measures ensure dedicated controller staffing and supervisory oversight during LUAW operations and reinforce the FAA’s commitment to maintaining the highest safety standards. This will not impact airport operations.

Dedicated Local Control: The local control position responsible for arriving and departing aircraft must not be combined with any non-local control position.

Stand-Alone Watch Supervision: A dedicated watch supervision position must be staffed and cannot be combined with any other position. This strengthens existing guidance by making stand-alone watch supervision mandatory.

The controversy gained attention after a radio exchange at Albuquerque International Sunport (ABQ). According to TheTravel, a controller told a Southwest Airlines crew about the new nationwide requirement, warning it could slow departures during the busiest travel time of the Thanksgiving rush. The controller described the restriction as something that would last forever, although the FAA's official notice did not use that wording.

Importantly, the FAA's stated objective is to improve runway safety, not reduce airport capacity. Having a dedicated supervisor overseeing operations should help prevent distractions and improve situational awareness when aircraft are positioned on active runways. The FAA's existing procedures also emphasize that Line Up and Wait is not takeoff clearance and that aircraft should not normally remain in that position for more than 90 seconds without further instructions.

But there is also an important clarification: the official notice lists June 9, 2027, as its cancellation date. Therefore, describing the measure as an indefinite or permanent prohibition is misleading. The actual impact will depend on staffing levels at individual towers and how frequently they can provide the additional supervisory position.

FAA ties delayed pay to efficiency metrics that demand more on position time amid a 3,000 controller shortfall.

The FAA is attempting to address its longstanding air traffic controller shortage through an ambitious recruitment campaign, including an unusual effort to attract video gamers. In October 2026, the agency announced that it had hired 2,235 controller trainees during the fiscal year, exceeding its recruitment target. The campaign reportedly attracted more than 12,000 qualified applicants within just 24 hours, demonstrating the potential of targeting candidates with strong multitasking and decision-making abilities.

However, recruiting additional candidates does not immediately solve the staffing problem. According to the FAA's 2026 workforce plan, becoming a fully certified controller can take more than two years, depending on the complexity of the assigned facility. The agency has set recruitment targets of 2,300 trainees for fiscal year 2027 and 2,400 for 2028, while expanding training capacity and modernizing its workforce management procedures.

As a result, the new Line Up and Wait requirements could create additional operational pressure before the benefits of increased recruitment become apparent. Although the measure is intended to strengthen runway safety, airports with limited staffing may have fewer opportunities to use an efficiency-enhancing procedure. For Thanksgiving travelers, the immediate concern is that an already busy aviation network could face additional departure bottlenecks during the holiday rush.

#6086. American AAdvantage Business Program: How To Earn Bonus Loyalty Points & Miles

American Airlines offers a small business rewards program, known as the AAdvantage Business program. This is a great way to earn extra rewards for your travel on American, including qualifying for bonus Loyalty Points and miles.

Best of all, eligibility for the program is surprisingly simple, assuming you have the Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard® (learn more). There’s often even a bonus for new AAdvantage Business members, making it even more rewarding.

In this post, I’d like to take a look at all of the details of the AAdvantage Business program, as many people find it to be quite complicated. Note that AAdvantage Business was launched in 2023, replacing the previous American Business Extra program, which no longer exists.

AAdvantage Business is the name of American Airlines’ business rewards program. This allows you to earn extra rewards in a business account, in addition to the rewards you can earn through your own AAdvantage account. Best of all, you have quite a bit of flexibility in terms of distributing the rewards. Let’s go over the details of how this works.

The AAdvantage Business program has a pretty straightforward rewards structure, as it rewards members with both Loyalty Points and AAdvantage miles. With the AAdvantage Business program, you earn the following rewards, which will post within 72 hours of an eligible flight:

Let me emphasize that business travelers only earn Loyalty Points through AAdvantage Business when the business is currently eligible to transfer miles, and that requires either having the Citi AAdvantage Business Card, or having at least five unique travelers who have credited flights to the AAdvantage Business account, totaling at least $5,000 in flight revenue, over the course of a year (the credit card method is obviously easier).

Just to clarify a few additional points about AAdvantage Business rewards:

These rewards are all in addition to the standard rewards that AAdvantage members receive:

Just to be crystal clear, an Executive Platinum member ordinarily earns 11 Loyalty Points per dollar spent on airfare, while if enrolled in the AAdvantage Business program, they’d earn 12 Loyalty Points per dollar spent. There’s no reason to leave those bonus rewards on the table!

In order to be eligible to participate in the AAdvantage Business program, you need to have a business in the United States or Canada with a Federal Employer Identification Number (FEIN) or Business Number. Even small businesses are eligible for this program.

The exceptions are that travel agencies, consolidators, wholesalers, and other sellers of travel, aren’t eligible to participate in AAdvantage Business. On top of that, AAdvantage Business technically can’t be used for leisure travel.

You accrue rewards in the AAdvantage Business program without any minimums, and then you can transfer the rewards to individual members, so that they can then redeem them out of their own accounts. In order to transfer the miles in the AAdvantage Business account to an individual AAdvantage account, you need to meet one of two requirements:

The AAdvantage Business program creates a huge incentive to get the Citi AAdvantage Business Card. That’s because just having the card allows many people to unlock the value of the AAdvantage Business program — there’s no need to actually use the card for your spending, but just having it is all that’s needed to redeem AAdvantage Business program rewards with no minimum on the number of travelers or revenue.

There are several potentially useful perks to this card, and on top of that, the card is offering a great welcome bonus, which is the reason that I applied for the card (and got approved), as that’s a nice incentive, beyond the value of access to the AAdvantage Business program.

It’s worth understanding how closely this card is actually integrated into the AAdvantage Business program:

For American frequent flyers with a small business, this creates a strong incentive to get the card. The card has a reasonable annual fee that’s waived the first year, and just having the card will allow many people to earn a sizable number of bonus miles.

If you’re curious about how the AAdvantage Business program works in practice, let me share some screenshots, for those who are more visual. Once you have an AAdvantage Business account, you’ll automatically become the travel manager for the account, and that means you can invite others to join your account (these should be people who work for your company, but there’s no verification process, as far as I know).

I should also mention that you can designate others to be travel managers as well, so that they can also invite others, transfer miles to people, etc. Travel managers must also be AAdvantage members who are adults and are residents of the United States or Canada.

To go through the process of inviting others to join your account, you’ll want to click “Invite people,” and then once they accept your invitation, they’ll show up on your account.

If someone’s AAdvantage account is linked to an AAdvantage Business program account, you’ll see that when you go to make a booking on aa.com, you’ll be asked for your “Travel type,” and can select “Business” or “Personal.” If you select “Business,” you’ll see that the company name populates, and you can select the name of the traveler.

Note that AAdvantage Business bookings are limited to one passenger, so if you have multiple people traveling, you’ll need to book as separate reservations. Also, to state the obvious, AAdvantage award tickets don’t qualify.

While the Loyalty Points from flights will post directly to the AAdvantage account of the member, the redeemable miles will post to the AAdvantage Business program account (the same is true for miles earned on the Citi AAdvantage Business Card). If you want to redeem miles, the only option is to transfer them to individual members, as you can’t redeem the miles directly out of the AAdvantage Business account.

If you’re eligible to transfer those miles, you’ll see the mileage balance listed, plus a “Transfer miles” button. There’s also a dashboard that shows your eligible number of travelers and eligible spending. However, as you can see above, I’ve met the transfer conditions even though I haven’t met the required threshold, since I have the Citi AAdvantage Business Card.

The process of transferring miles is super easy. You’ll just enter how many miles you want to transfer, and who you want to transfer them to, and then they should post to the AAdvantage account instantly.

My general take on the AAdvantage Business program is as follows:

The program basically offers an incremental 1.5% return on your American spending, since you earn one extra AAdvantage mile per dollar spent, and based on my miles & points valuations, those are worth 1.5 cents each. On top of that, the program offers an incremental Loyalty Point per dollar spent — that will have no value to some, while it will have significant value to others, depending on the extent to which you’re pursuing status in the coming year.

It is interesting the extent to which American has basically given up on corporate travel. American’s priority is getting people to book direct and keeping distribution costs as low as possible. So this program is intended as the major incentive for most small businesses.

American Airlines offers the AAdvantage Business program. With this program, the business earns one AAdvantage mile per dollar spent on eligible airfare, while the individual traveler earns one Loyalty Point per dollar spent. In order to participate and be able to redeem miles, you need a business with at least five registered employees who have each taken at least one eligible flight, along with $5,000 in annual spending, or you need to have the Citi AAdvantage Business Card.

Yes, but only if you choose not to travel. U.S. Department of Transportation rules require airlines to issue prompt refunds to passengers whose flight is canceled or significantly delayed. But passengers aren't eligible for a refund if they take a later flight.

Yes. DOT refund rules govern all flight disruptions, even flights canceled or delayed because of bad weather.

If the airline owes you a refund, federal rules require the carrier to refund your money within seven days if you paid by credit card, or 20 days if you paid by a different means.

It's been a chaotic couple of weeks for air travel in America, between tech outages and bad weather. Now, the holiday rush is here.

And with millions of travelers heading to airports, it's an important time to brush up on one of the most important rights that passengers have: getting a refund.

In the U.S., passengers don't have a ton of protection when it comes to delays and cancellations.

However, the federal government does have clear rules about when an airline must issue a refund.

Let's quickly walk through when you're owed a refund — and when you're not — so you can know what to ask for the next time you encounter flight trouble.

Read more: Is air travel ready for the holidays? The meltdown is over, but worries persist

For domestic flights, as well as international flights departing or arriving in the U.S., you’re covered by the rules of the U.S. Department of Transportation.

Under the DOT flight refund policy, you are entitled to a refund, no questions asked, if your flight is canceled and you ultimately choose not to travel. It doesn’t matter whether the cancellation was the airline’s fault or due to something beyond its control, like bad weather.

The policy applies to any unflown portion of your ticket.

The DOT refund rules also apply when a flight is significantly delayed or when the airline makes a significant schedule change.

Again, though, this is only if you choose not to travel.

According to federal law, a significant delay occurs when a domestic flight arrives at its destination at least three hours late, or an international flight arrives six hours late.

That also applies when the airline decides to change a flight's schedule.

Here's the big catch: You're only owed a refund if you choose not to travel, and you don't accept rebooking.

Your right to a refund is helpful if you run into a flight cancellation and delay and choose to:

The federal refund rules are less helpful if you need to fly to your destination and don't have a better backup option.

If your airline cancels your 8 a.m. flight and rebooks you on a later flight — even if it's a lot later —  your carrier would not technically owe you a refund if you agree to take that later flight.

In recent years, you may have heard about the federal government passing stricter rules when it comes to flight refunds.

That did happen, but the rules still aren't ironclad.

The actual criteria for when passengers are owed a refund didn't meaningfully change, though.

By law, airline refunds are expected "promptly" — within seven days for passengers who paid by credit card and within 20 days for those who paid by another means.

Airlines are allowed to offer passengers a voucher (or miles) instead of a refund.

However, refund-eligible passengers don’t have to accept a voucher. They can insist on simply getting their money back instead.

Know the fine print: Under the DOT's policy, if an airline wants to offer you miles when you're technically due a refund, they have to clearly disclose that.

Think carefully before accepting airline miles instead of a cash refund. You'll want to make sure you're truly getting better value. Consult TPG’s points and miles valuations to check the value of what the airline is offering in loyalty currency.

Remember: Airlines tend to devalue miles over time, so if you do accept miles, we'd suggest using them as soon as possible.

Compensation for things like meals, an unexpected hotel stay or an Uber ride in the event of a flight delay or cancellation falls under a different category than refunds.

Many airlines make guarantees about what they’ll provide in the event of a cancellation or significant delay. Those promises are laid out on the DOT’s airline customer service dashboard.

These promises are more discretionary forms of compensation. In other words, the airlines don't technically have to offer those meal vouchers or hotel bookings. Think of this as more of a goodwill gesture that the airlines have promised their customers they'll provide ... depending on the circumstances.

Also, airlines generally offer compensation only for hotel, meal and ground transportation when it's a "controllable" disruption — in other words, when it's the airline's fault.

I wouldn't count on that hotel voucher if your flight is canceled due to a winter storm or air traffic control delays.

This is where a credit card that offers travel insurance protections can be crucial (and, for me, really eliminates the financial stress of flight troubles).

Check out TPG’s guide to passenger rights for a better sense of what you might be owed.

Just prior to leaving office, the Biden administration proposed rules requiring airlines to pay passengers additional cash compensation when the carrier caused a cancellation or major delay.

However, the Trump administration opted not to move forward with that measure.

It can be challenging to keep track of airline policies, but the federal rules that govern refunds are relatively straightforward.

You are owed a refund for any unused portion of your ticket if your flight is canceled, significantly delayed or has a significant schedule change (no matter the reason) and you ultimately choose not to travel with that airline. That refund should come automatically and within seven days if you paid by credit card, or 20 days if you paid using a different method.

It’s likely you are not entitled to a refund if:

Passengers who feel that an airline hasn't followed protocol or has unfairly denied a refund request can file a complaint with the DOT.

#6084. Democrats nominate Jeffries to be House speaker, a historic first

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no announced opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

“It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries said at a press conference following the election.

While Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

“Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get big things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”

Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”

Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

“This is the beginning of a new bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., said at the press conference.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

Jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the new majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

At his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

“We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

“I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”

Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had said they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

Pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

The entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

Jeffries said Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”

Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

“House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he said at his news conference.

#6083. Dozens Fall Ill On Two Condor Flights To Frankfurt, Triggering Mass Casualty Response

Dozens of passengers across two separate transatlantic Condor flights became ill, causing a mass casualty incident response at Frankfurt Airport (FRA), as reported by aeroTELEGRAPH. While this is still being investigated, there’s a theory as to what happened, given what all passengers had in common…

On Saturday, November 21, 2026, Condor operated two flights from La Romana, Dominican Republic (LRM), to Frankfurt, Germany (FRA). Both flights were operated by the Airbus A330-900neo, with as many as 620 passengers onboard.

Flight DE3705 took off at 8:03PM on Saturday and landed at 9:23AM on Sunday, while DE3845 took off at 9:14PM on Saturday and landed at 10:35AM on Sunday. The flights had one thing in common, which is that between them, dozens of passengers became ill.

The illnesses onboard were so bad that a “MANV 25” response was triggered at Frankfurt Airport. That’s a German emergency response alert for a mass casualty incident — “Massenanfall von Verletzten” (though fortunately there were no fatalities here).

Passengers onboard were screened by medical teams, and one person on each flight was taken to a local hospital, while others are being monitored.

It’s not uncommon to hear stories of multiple people becoming sick on flights. Sometimes it’s a fume event, sometimes it could be a case of food poisoning (though it doesn’t usually happen that fast), etc. So what’s going on here, that people on two separate Condor flights became ill?

Well, the passengers on these two flights had one thing in common — they all came off the AidaBella cruise ship in La Romana, and then these flights were sold as part of the cruise package.

So while this is still being investigated, a norovirus outbreak on the cruise ship is believed to be the likely culprit. I’ve gotta say, an airplane seems like a pretty unpleasant place to come down with a gastrointestinal illness, so I imagine the lavatory situation onboard probably wasn’t great.

Dozens of passengers on two separate Condor flights between the Dominican Republic and Germany around the same time became ill, triggering an emergency response at Frankfurt Airport, which included a couple of people being hospitalized.

While it remains to be seen what caused this, the belief is that it could be some sort of a norovirus outbreak, based on the symptoms, as well as the fact that the passengers had all come off the same cruise ship. I hope everyone makes a quick recovery.

What do you make of this Condor incident?

#6082. How The Airbus A350 Survives Environmental Stress During The Longest Flights In The World

Before entering commercial service, the Airbus A350 had to prove it could withstand some of the harshest conditions on Earth. Airbus needed to establish how its engines, systems, and structure would respond to extreme temperatures and demanding operating conditions. From the freezing Canadian Arctic to the scorching deserts of the United Arab Emirates and the high-altitude airports of Bolivia, Airbus deliberately pushed its new widebody aircraft to its limits.

Through these trials, Airbus sought to ensure that the A350 could operate safely and reliably across a wide range of environments. The A350 has since become a key aircraft for ultra-long-haul operations, including Singapore Airlines' nonstop flights between Singapore and New York. So, how did Airbus test the A350, and what did these trials reveal about the aircraft's capabilities?

Before entering commercial service, every new aircraft must undergo extensive testing and certification to demonstrate compliance with aviation safety standards. For Airbus aircraft, the main certification authority is the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), while the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) validates the design for the US market. The process begins with the Type Certificate (TC), which confirms that an aircraft's design meets the applicable airworthiness requirements. Manufacturers must also hold the relevant production approvals, while each individual aircraft requires a Certificate of Airworthiness (CoA) before entering service. Airlines must additionally meet operational requirements, including crew training, maintenance arrangements, and any necessary authorizations.

The certification process also varies depending on the aircraft's design and available configurations. For example, Airbus' A320neo Family certification program covered six airframe and engine combinations. The A319neo, A320neo and A321neo each required validation of their airframes, systems and two available engine options: the CFM International LEAP-1A and Pratt & Whitney Geared Turbofan (GTF). These campaigns also verified whether the aircraft met their performance targets for fuel consumption and range, reflecting improvements from the new engines and Sharklet wingtip devices.

For the A350-900, Airbus completed its flight-test and certification campaign in just over 14 months, setting an industry record for the program's completion time. Five test aircraft accumulated more than 2,600 flight hours, during which Airbus evaluated the aircraft's handling characteristics, systems, performance, and reliability. The campaign culminated in the A350-900 receiving Type Certification from EASA and the FAA in 2014. However, the program also involved specialized environmental testing in Canada, the United Arab Emirates, and Bolivia, along with controlled temperature trials at the McKinley Climatic Laboratory in the United States. These tests would establish how the A350 performed in conditions far beyond those encountered during routine airline operations.

In January 2014, Airbus took its A350-900 MSN3 development aircraft to Iqaluit, Canada, to conduct cold-weather trials in temperatures as low as -28°C. A team of 48 Airbus specialists assessed how the aircraft's engines and systems performed in freezing conditions. One key test involved starting the engines and auxiliary power unit (APU) after a cold soak, during which the aircraft was left exposed to extremely low temperatures for an extended period. The team also conducted system checks, low-speed taxiing, rejected takeoffs, and a local test flight to verify the aircraft's performance.

Three years later, Airbus returned to Iqaluit with the larger A350-1000, which underwent five days of intensive ground and flight testing in temperatures ranging from -28°C to -37°C. Alongside these Arctic trials, Airbus also used the McKinley Climatic Laboratory at Eglin Air Force Base in Florida, becoming the first Airbus aircraft to undergo testing at the facility. Unlike Iqaluit, where engineers depended on natural weather, the laboratory's climate-controlled hangar allowed Airbus to simulate temperatures from -40°C to +40°C under controlled conditions.

However, extreme cold was only one part of the A350's environmental testing program. While the Canadian trials focused on the aircraft's ability to operate in freezing conditions, Airbus also needed to assess its performance in extreme heat and at high-altitude airports. This took the A350 to Al Ain in the United Arab Emirates and La Paz in Bolivia, where high temperatures and reduced air density presented a different set of operational challenges.

Airbus has introduced new operational limitations affecting its narrowbody aircraft equipped with PW1100 engines.

While freezing temperatures presented one challenge, Airbus also needed to demonstrate that the A350 could operate safely in extreme heat. In July 2017, the manufacturer sent its A350-1000 test aircraft, MSN065, to Al Ain International Airport in the United Arab Emirates for a three-day hot-weather testing campaign. Conducted between 4 and 7 July, the trials exposed the aircraft to temperatures exceeding 40°C, reaching as high as 48°C. The objective was to assess how the aircraft's systems performed in scorching conditions, particularly the Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engines and cabin air-conditioning systems.

One main concern was whether the aircraft could maintain comfortable cabin temperatures on the ground, where cooling systems must cope with intense external heat. Engineers also assessed engine performance, as higher temperatures reduce air density and affect engine thrust and takeoff performance. This can increase the runway distance required for departure, particularly at airports with shorter runways. The importance of these limitations became evident in June 2017, when extreme temperatures in Phoenix, Arizona, led to dozens of flight cancellations involving regional aircraft with lower maximum operating temperature limits.

According to Airbus, the A350-1000 successfully met all the parameters established for its Al Ain campaign, demonstrating its readiness to operate in extreme heat. However, high temperatures are not the only factor that reduces air density. Airports situated thousands of meters above sea level present similar performance challenges, even when outside temperatures are considerably lower. To assess these conditions, Airbus also conducted high-altitude testing in Bolivia.

Airbus also took the A350 to El Alto International Airport in La Paz, Bolivia, situated approximately 4,061 meters (13,325 feet) above sea level. At this elevation, air density is roughly 40% lower than at sea level under comparable standard conditions, creating significant challenges for aircraft performance. Thinner air reduces the amount of oxygen available to the engines, limiting the thrust they can produce, while also reducing the lift generated by the wings at a given airspeed. Consequently, aircraft generally require higher true airspeeds and longer take-off distances to become airborne.

High-altitude testing allows Airbus to evaluate how aircraft systems and engines respond to these demanding conditions. One particularly important assessment involves engine starting, which becomes more challenging as air density decreases. Engineers also examine thrust response, takeoff and climb performance, and the aircraft's handling characteristics. Jean-Philippe Cottet, Airbus' head of design development flight tests, identified starting engines at high altitude as one of the main reasons the manufacturer conducts trials specifically in La Paz.

The A350-900 and A350-1000 were among the aircraft Airbus tested at La Paz, which has also hosted other Airbus development programs. These evaluations help establish the aircraft's operational limitations and demonstrate its ability to perform safely at high-elevation airports. Together with the cold-weather trials in Canada and hot-weather testing in the UAE, the campaign provided evidence of the A350's capabilities across markedly different operating environments.

The Airbus A350 has a service ceiling of around 43,000 ft.

Beyond extreme weather testing, Airbus also needed to demonstrate how the A350 would perform during extended commercial operations. As part of its certification campaign, the manufacturer conducted a global route-proving program, visiting 14 major airports across four separate trips and covering approximately 81,700 nautical miles in 180 flight hours. Airbus also introduced an Early Long Flights (ELF) program, which went beyond regulatory certification requirements. These simulated commercial services carried Airbus employees acting as passengers, with airline flight crews operating a fully equipped cabin to evaluate onboard systems under realistic conditions. Such testing helped prepare the A350 for demanding long-haul operations, including Singapore Airlines' nonstop services between Singapore and New York, which use the A350-900ULR and can exceed 18 hours.

The A350's long-range capabilities are also central to Qantas' Project Sunrise, which aims to introduce nonstop flights from Sydney to London and New York using specially configured A350-1000ULR aircraft. Compared with the standard A350-1000, the Project Sunrise variant incorporates an additional fuel tank with approximately 5,283 gallons (20,000 liters) of capacity to support longer journeys. The A350's composite fuselage also resists corrosion and fatigue, while its cabin pressurization and environmental control systems allow a cabin altitude of about 6,000 feet and higher humidity than many older aircraft. These features are particularly relevant on flights lasting 18 hours or more, where passenger comfort becomes increasingly important.

However, the ability to withstand extreme temperatures and remain airborne for extended periods is only part of the challenge. Ultra-long-haul operations also require careful management of crew fatigue, passenger wellbeing, maintenance schedules, and operational reliability. As airlines prepare to operate flights approaching 20 hours, the question is no longer simply how far an aircraft can fly, but rather how comfortably and efficiently passengers and crew can endure the journey.

While the A350's certification trials demonstrated its ability to withstand extreme operating conditions, flights approaching 20 hours present another challenge: passenger wellbeing. Ahead of its Project Sunrise services, Qantas partnered with researchers from the University of Sydney's Charles Perkins Centre to investigate ways of reducing jet lag on ultra-long-haul flights. During experimental flights lasting approximately 20 hours, researchers monitored 23 volunteers wearing tracking devices as they followed specially designed schedules for meals, cabin lighting, sleep, and movement. Initial findings suggested that passengers following these routines experienced less severe self-reported jet lag, better sleep quality during the flight and improved cognitive performance in the two days following arrival compared with those following conventional inflight routines.

Qantas plans to incorporate these findings into its A350-1000ULR operations, including tailored cabin lighting, recommended meal and rest schedules, and a dedicated Wellbeing Zone where premium economy and economy passengers can stretch and move around. The airline also expects its nonstop Project Sunrise services to reduce total journey times by more than three hours compared with connecting flights. While Singapore Airlines' existing A350-900ULR operations have already demonstrated the aircraft family's suitability for ultra-long-haul services, Project Sunrise will provide another important test of its capabilities.

Ultimately, the success of these routes will depend not only on aircraft reliability and commercial performance, but also on how effectively airlines can make journeys approaching 20 hours comfortable for passengers and manageable for crews.
