#6081. Qatar Airways Airbus A321LRs With Flat Bed Business Class Launching Soon

In the coming weeks, Qatar Airways is expected to take delivery of its first Airbus A321LR, which will be the carrier’s first narrow body aircraft featuring latest generation interiors, including flat beds. The airline will be introducing a “mini-Qsuite” type product on these planes, and we’ve now learned exactly when this new premium narrow body jet will enter service.

Qatar Airways currently has a total of 50 factory fresh Airbus A321-family aircraft on order. This includes 10 A321LRs and 40 A321neos — both of those are latest generation aircraft, with the A321LR featuring additional range.

The expectation is that the first A321LR will be delivered in the coming weeks, before the end of 2026. The 10 A321LRs should join the fleet pretty quickly, and will then be followed by the A321neos. The A321LRs will be configured with 160 seats, including 16 business class seats and 144 economy class seats.

The A321LR has a maximum range of 4,000 nautical miles, so it can be used for many destinations in Europe, Africa, and Asia. Below is a map showing the rough range from Doha (though in reality it won’t be quite as far, accounting for winds, fuel reserves, etc.).

Now, for those paying close attention, I should acknowledge that Qatar Airways briefly flew six leased, all-economy A321neos, but those were just intended as a temporary solution, and are now flying for Sun PhuQuoc Airways, which is running an interesting operation.

Qatar Airways’ A321neo-family aircraft order goes back a long time, and involved a lot of drama. The order was first announced in 2011, then the airline reconfirmed and upsized it in 2017. However, then former Qatar Airways CEO Akbar Al Baker got into a fight with Airbus over A350 production quality, and refused to take delivery of any Airbus planes.

That turned into a massive court battle, which was eventually resolved. But in the process, Qatar Airways lost all of its Airbus delivery slots, which is why these planes are coming way later than initially expected.

Qatar Airways has been promising all along that it would introduce some sort of a next generation flat bed business class product on its Airbus A321LRs. As you’d expect, business class seats on narrow bodies sometimes differ from those on wide bodies, due to differing cabin constraints.

What can we expect onboard these Qatar Airways A321LRs in business class? Executive Traveller quotes Qatar Airways CEO Hamad Ali Al-Khater as saying that the new business class product will be based on the STELIA Aerospace OPERA platform.

These planes will boast 16 business class seats, in a 1-1 configuration. This product offers reverse herringbone seats, and Qatar Airways plans to have doors at each seat as well, of course with its customized finishes.

The launch customer for the STELIA Aerospace OPERA platform was Air France on its A350s. However, that’s the wide body version of the seat, which is modified from the narrow body version.

When it comes to the narrow body version of the STELIA Aerospace OPERA platform, ITA Airways was the launch customer, on its A321neos.

This is also the product that Etihad is installing on its A321LRs. ITA Airways and Etihad don’t have doors in business class, but Qatar Airways does plan to offer it. Etihad also markets the first row of the cabin as first class (and that has doors), but I wouldn’t expect Qatar Airways to do something similar.

This is about as good as narrow body business class seats get, as it’s generally preferred to the herringbone seats you’ll find on other carriers, like JetBlue A321LRs, American A321XLRs, etc.

Qatar Airways now seems pretty certain about the delivery of its upcoming Airbus A321LRs, as the airline has officially put the first routes on sale, as flagged by AeroRoutes:

When you pull up the above flights, you’ll now see the seat map for the A321LR, which confirms the 16-seat business class cabin.

In the coming weeks, Qatar Airways is expected to take delivery of its first of 10 Airbus A321LRs. This will be the first custom designed next generation narrow body that the airline takes delivery of. We knew the airline would offer flat bed seats on these planes, and now we have the details of that.

The airline has gone with the STELIA Aerospace OPERA platform, the same product you’ll find on similar planes of Etihad and ITA Airways. However, unlike those airlines, Qatar Airways will have doors in business class. The planes will enter service by very early 2027, flying from Doha to both Vienna and Zurich.

What do you make of Qatar Airways’ upcoming A321LRs, and the planned interiors?

#6080. Dems express ‘points of anxiety’ over Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi

President Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of issues even as he appears politically weakened at home.

Trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

The U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one issue with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

“As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he said. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

Still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”

Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., said part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

“They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” said Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

“I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump said Monday. “I think he's backing down.”

Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a big reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

Senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”

“I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine said. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”

During remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

“Enforcement of the new rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat said, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

“Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he said. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”

But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

He stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, said Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”

Trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the company’s president and CEO. He also said he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

The administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”

Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”

“Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear issues dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”

Have you ever butted heads with a partner because you wanted to plan a jam-packed vacation itinerary and they preferred to lounge on the beach? Have you ever argued with family or friends about whether to book a local Airbnb or an all-inclusive resort? When flying solo, you don't need to worry about these dilemmas — and that's far from the only benefit of solo travel.

However, planning a trip on your own can feel daunting, especially if it's your first time. That's why I've rounded up some of TPG's favorite destinations for first-time solo travelers. No matter what kind of traveler you are and what you're looking for on your maiden voyage, this list is sure to inspire you.

Related: The 12 best places to travel solo

While Mexico often conjures images of all-inclusive hotels and long beach days, the cultural and culinary hub of Oaxaca goes deeper. TPG managing editor Lyndsey Matthews just got back from a solo trip here and raves about the travel-worthy food scene and captivating art and history.

“The historic center of Oaxaca is easily walkable and full of coffee shops, art galleries and ceramic stores to pop in and out of at your own pace and convenience,” she says. “It was also super easy to make friends on the few tours I booked — I did a nighttime street food tour with Culinary Backstreets and a long day trip to Hierve del Agua that I booked on Viator, and I ended up running into the people I met at bakeries and markets the rest of the week.”

Related: 5 detour destinations in Mexico beyond the tourist hot spots

Whatever type of solo trip you’re dreaming of, France is worth considering.

TPG principal spokesperson Clint Henderson recommends Paris. It may be known as the City of Love, but that doesn’t mean you can’t enjoy it on your own — especially if you’re a foodie or art lover. Snack on fresh-baked croissants in between museum visits (the Musee du quai Branly, which features non-Western art from around the world, is a must-see).

If you’d prefer a slower pace, Lauren Wassum raves about Provence: “There are plenty of villages to explore where you can get in touch with yourself through slow and intentional living.” But this isn’t to say there is nothing to do. “You can walk Van Gogh’s footsteps in Arles and Saint-Rémy, take a provencal cooking class or even tour the lavender fields when in they are in bloom in the Luberon Valley.”

To really push yourself out of your comfort zone, try Japan for your first solo trip. Japan’s culture and traditions are so different from the U.S., it will catapult you out of your day-to-day life a little faster than most destinations.

TPG senior writer Tanner Saunders loves the Land of the Rising Sun as a solo destination. “Tokyo is massive, sure, but it's relatively easy to figure out how to get around, the people are mostly so kind, it's super safe and dining alone is so common.” And don’t worry if you can’t read Japanese; English is common in most tourist areas.

Japan may seem small, but its islands are incredibly diverse. There’s something for every type of traveler — from the snow-dusted ski capital of Hokkaido to the southernmost island of Okinawa, sometimes known as “the Hawaii of Japan.”

Related: When is the best time to visit Japan?

Senior editor Christine Gallipeau recommends New Zealand for first-time solo travelers, citing the country’s safety record and the Kiwis’ trademark friendliness.

“I was there during the Rugby World Cup and had a last-minute issue with lodging,” she says. “One of the local airports let me and my friends just crash in the rental car office for the night, and later in Wellington, a stranger opened their home to us since hostels and hotels were sold out.”

It takes a while to get here, but you’ll be rewarded with peace, quiet and the sense of being truly alone.

Most visitors agree road tripping is the best way to see New Zealand, so you’ll need to rent a car (and be prepared to drive on the left side). You can see the highlights in just a few days, or spend weeks exploring and not run out of things to do.

Related: Explore some of New Zealand's most beautiful regions at these Rosewood lodges

If you’d like to stay a little closer to home for your first solo trip, Costa Rica is relatively easy to reach from the U.S. while still feeling a world away.

It’s among Latin America’s most popular solo travel destinations thanks, in part, to its friendly locals. “Everyone is sooo welcoming,” says TPG social media manager Maren Gimnes, “plus it’s safe and easy to get around.”

With beaches on one side and wildlife-rich rainforests on the other, not to mention volcanoes and hot springs, solo travelers can get their fill of both relaxation and adventure.

Try basing yourself in Tamarindo if you’re after sun, surf and sand. If wildlife is your main goal, head to Monteverde Cloud Forest or Manuel Antonio National Park. Thrill seekers will want to focus on La Fortuna, the country’s adventure capital.

Related: How to visit Costa Rica on points and miles

Many European cities are great candidates for first-time solo trips, but Ireland’s lively capital city stands out for its welcoming pub culture and manageable size. TPG social media manager Annie Black loves it because Dublin is “very easy to navigate and has lots of fun free things to do.”

If you’re hoping to socialize with locals and fellow travelers, Dublin’s welcoming pub culture is a must. Head to the bustling Temple Bar neighborhood (or any pub, really) for a pint of Guinness or Bulmer’s and some foot-stomping trad music.

Plus, plentiful day trips and group tours make it easy for solo travelers to explore nearby attractions like the gorgeous Wicklow Mountains and the jaw-dropping Giant’s Causeway without the hassle of renting a car.

Related: What it's like flying Aer Lingus business class across the Atlantic

If you’re ready to venture a little farther afield, TPG principal Eric Rosen highlights Cape Town as a great spot for first-time visitors, saying it’s “very navigable and safe for solo travelers.”

Cape Town has all the benefits of a city trip plus easy access to outdoor pursuits like hiking, mountain bike trails, beaches and even penguins. Rideshares are readily available and affordable for getting around town, or you can easily explore outside the city by renting a car, hiring a driver or joining an organized group tour.

Sea Point and De Waterkant/Green Point neighborhoods are great choices for solo travelers wanting a safe, walkable base close to the beach. If you’d rather be within easy reach of the restaurant and bar scene on Kloof Street, try Tamboerskloof.

Related: Africa's first Edition hotel is opening in Cape Town next year

Vietnam is a Southeast Asian sliver of adventure, culture and more. Plus, it’s quite affordable — even if you’re not splitting the cost of your hotel with a travel companion. Most meals will run you between $5 and $10.

There’s truly something for everyone: The UNESCO World Heritage Site of Ha Long Bay; the delightfully chaotic capital of Hanoi; and the hip beach town of Da Nang, where expats from all over the world relax.

You won’t want to leave without sampling some of the local cuisine. There’s pho and banh mi, of course, but don’t miss other local dishes like bun cha (pork with dipping broth) and cha ca (turmeric-marinated fish). Wash it all down with a beer at Hanoi’s Train Street, where you can eat while watching an active railway run back and forth inches from your trackside café.

Related: A new Hilton just opened one of Vietnam's best cities

There’s a reason (several, in fact) that Iceland is a perennial favorite for solo travelers. English is nearly ubiquitous, and the country’s manageable size and well-developed infrastructure make it easy to get around. It’s also one of the safest countries on the planet — so safe, it’s said Iceland has more horses than police officers.

Nature lovers can bask in a huge variety of landscapes, from hiking across glaciers to soaking in geothermal hot springs to snorkeling between tectonic plates. Meanwhile, travelers seeking nightlife and connection can revel in downtown Reykjavik, which also has a booming LGBTQIA+ scene.

“You really can’t go wrong with any Nordic country,” TPG managing editor Lyndsey Matthews says. “English is widely spoken, plus they’re all very safe countries, so I’ve always been comfortable whether it’s a super remote destination or a big city.”

Related: Delta Air Lines adds Iceland nonstops from Boston hub

Whether you’re looking for epic underwater adventures or a few days of beach bumming, look no further than the Central American oasis of Belize.

Despite its small size, Belize has a big reputation for some of the world’s best snorkeling and scuba diving. Check some adventures off your bucket list by diving the Great Blue Hole or swimming with nurse sharks in Shark Ray Alley.

If you’d rather spend your vacation on land — perhaps in a hammock with a good book and a cold drink — head out on a ferry to one of the many islands, or cays, like car-free Caye Caulker. The island's motto is “Go Slow,” and that’s all you need to know.

Related: Belize's best all-inclusive resorts

When traveling solo, you can go, do, see and eat exactly what you choose — whether that's a culture-filled city trip, an epic outdoor adventure, a relaxing beach break or a little of everything. This list has all the above so you can choose your dream solo destination.

Need more inspo for your first solo trip? Don't miss our roundups of the best places to travel solo in the US, the top destinations for a solo weekend getaway and the best cruise lines for solo travelers.

#6077. American Blocking Domestic Saver Awards Close To Departure (Within Six Days)

In May 2026, we saw American introduce a major new restriction for award travel, which had the biggest implications for those redeeming on American through partner programs, like Alaska Atmos Rewards or British Airways Club (in other words, anyone redeeming through a program other than American AAdvantage).

With this, American started to restrict its own saver level award availability close to departure. Initially, all domestic nonstop saver awards within six days of departure were pulled. In recent days, it looks like American has expanded this to all domestic connecting itineraries as well, so I’d like to cover those details (thanks to azbobcat for flagging this).

Historically, American has been by far the best of the “big three” US carriers when it comes to making award seats on its own flights available, especially on domestic and short haul international flights. American actually releases a good amount of saver award seats across cabins, and it’s one of the things that makes AAdvantage better than the competition.

However, in May 2026, we saw American introduce a major change to how it releases award space to partner frequent flyer programs. Long story short, American started blocking all nonstop, domestic saver award availability, for flights within six days (exactly 144 hours) of departure.

As soon as a flight gets to the point where it’s 144 hours until departure, you’ll see that the airline “turns off” its saver fare classes — I’m referring specifically to the “U” (saver business class award) and “T” (saver economy award) fare classes, which show up when searching on ExpertFlyer, for example.

Initially, this applied exclusively to nonstop, domestic award tickets, as connecting itineraries and all international itineraries (including short haul international ones) weren’t impacted by this. However, this seems to have now expanded to domestic connecting itineraries as well.

So any wholly domestic itinerary exclusively on American is no longer bookable at the saver level within six days of departure. International itineraries continue to be bookable within six days of departure, whether traveling nonstop or with a connection.

What would cause American to suddenly “shut off” saver awards for domestic routes within days of departure?

What’s interesting here is that the implications for AAdvantage members are limited. Yes, American has shut off awards in the saver fare classes, but that’s not to say that American isn’t making reasonably priced awards available within days of departure. American has long used some kind of dynamic award pricing concept for its own flights, regardless of whether or not there’s saver availability.

It’s just that any awards in the official saver fare buckets aren’t available, and therefore aren’t bookable with points belonging to partner programs.

So it sure seems to me that the intent here is to block award availability for those booking through partner programs, like Alaska Atmos Rewards or British Airways Club. It goes without saying that I absolutely hate this restriction, as someone who “funds” a vast majority of my domestic American travel using Atmos Rewards points. At the same time, I also have to say that I can’t blame American for this change, as the airline has just made it too easy.

I’ve been booking basically all my travel directly into American first class using Atmos Rewards points — I just set ExpertFlyer availability alerts for “U” class, it opens up a vast majority of the time, and then I book. It’s not surprising that American finally got a bit savvier.

American is now blocking all saver awards within exactly six days of departure for all domestic itineraries. This means within that timeframe, there’s no “U” or “T” availability, which corresponds to the saver business and economy award fare buckets, respectively. Initially this only applied to nonstop flights, while now it also applies to connecting itineraries.

For American AAdvantage members, the implications are limited, since American can still make reasonably priced awards available, just not formally in those fare buckets. The practical implications here are that partner programs just don’t have access to these award seats close to departure anymore.

What do you make of American’s six day rule on award tickets?

#6076. Southwest Airlines Plus Card Review: Modest Benefits For A Low Annual Fee

Southwest Airlines and Chase have a great portfolio of co-branded credit cards at a variety of “price points” (and by that I mean annual fees). In this post, I’d like to take a closer look at the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card, which is Southwest Airlines’ lowest annual fee credit card.

In my Southwest Plus Card review, I’ll cover the benefits and explain why now is a good time to consider this card if you want to use credit card spending to earn the Companion Pass. I’ll also explain why other Southwest cards can be better, and share a great alternative to earning Southwest Rapid Rewards points altogether.

Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card

Before I get into my Southwest Plus Card review, here are some of the key card details:

Here are my thoughts on the Southwest Plus Card’s pros and cons:

Let’s take a look at the Southwest Plus Card‘s welcome bonus, annual fee, and eligibility rules, as these are some of the most important factors to take into account if you’re considering applying.

The Southwest Plus Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus: Earn 80,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. This is one of the higher bonuses I’ve seen on this card recently, making now a particularly good time to apply.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each. So to me, the points from this welcome offer are worth $960.

In terms of Southwest credit card eligibility, the card isn’t available to anyone who currently has a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card, or anyone who has received a welcome bonus on a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible if you have a Southwest business credit card.

Beyond the restrictions related to which Southwest cards you have, keep in mind the general restrictions for Chase card approvals, including the 5/24 rule. However, there are increasing data points of this no longer being consistently enforced.

Another rule worth mentioning here involves how Southwest credit card welcome bonuses help you earn the Companion Pass, which lets you bring a companion with you on flights (both cash and award tickets) and pay just taxes and fees.

For a long time now, the points earned as part of Southwest credit card welcome bonuses have counted towards the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn the Companion Pass. But starting soon, credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward qualification.

You’ll need to apply for a card by December 2, 2026, for your welcome bonus to count toward the Companion Pass for a final time. So apply for this card now if you’re hoping to earn that perk with the help of credit card spending.

Now is also your last chance to get an annual boost of 10,000 Companion Pass qualifying points as a Southwest credit card holder. Starting next year, instead of a boost of 10,000 TQPs for having a Southwest card, you’ll get 10,000 TQPs if your TQP balance is 130,000 by December 31, 2027. That would be enough to get you to Platinum status, which will include unlimited Companion Pass trips as a benefit.

This change eliminates the easiest way to earn this valuable benefit, and it’s not the only new rule: referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending, and partner spending won’t count toward the Companion Pass either. In fact, Southwest’s rolling the Companion Pass into its highest elite tier, Platinum, and requiring either 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights to earn it.

The Southwest Plus Card has a $99 annual fee, and you can add authorized users to the card at no extra cost.

$99 is the lowest annual fee of any Southwest Airlines credit card. Looking at the high end, Southwest’s personal cards have annual fees of up to $229, and Southwest’s business cards have annual fees of up to $299.

The Southwest Plus Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s a solid card to use for purchases abroad.

As far as the Southwest Plus Card‘s rewards structure goes, the card offers the following:

Since I value Southwest Rapid Rewards points at 1.2 cents each, I think you get an effective return of 2.4% on purchases that qualify for 2x points, and a 1.2% return on everything else.

It’s nice that the card has some bonus categories, though there are ultimately more rewarding cards out there for everyday spending. Plus, a few of the non-Southwest bonus categories have an annual cap, which limits how useful this card is for maximizing your return on gas station and grocery store purchases.

I have a dedicated post that covers how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but let’s briefly look at how you can use the points you earn from the Southwest Plus Card.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, meaning that the value you get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. There are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, so the exact value can vary a bit.

Basic award fares tend to offer the best redemption value. You’ll also usually get the best value on international Southwest routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. I’ve been able to get about 2.0 cents per point on these redemptions.

Starting in spring 2027, Southwest will add points earning and redemption opportunities with select airline partners, which should make your Rapid Rewards points more valuable for international travel. The planned partners include Icelandair, China Airlines, and Etihad Airways — I look forward to seeing how these add value to the program.

One great thing about the Southwest Rapid Rewards program is that there are no change or cancellation fees, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d cancel and rebook rather than change.

The Southwest Plus Card offers some benefits that could make the card worth keeping long term. However, this is also Southwest’s lowest annual fee card, so it doesn’t have the most benefits. What are the ongoing perks of having this card?

The Southwest Plus Card gets the primary cardholder and up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation a first checked bag at no additional cost. Checked bags on Southwest cost $45 each way, so this can save you up to $90 roundtrip on checked bag fees per person. So with just one roundtrip flight per year, this benefit can almost offset the annual fee.

Southwest now charges for seat selection, so it’s helpful that the Southwest Plus Card includes complimentary standard seat selection starting 48 hours out from departure. This perk is based on availability, and it could save you around $20 to $40 per flight.

Another Southwest benefit is early boarding. You’ll be able to board with Group 5, or earlier if you have elite status or a fare or seat type that qualifies you for an earlier boarding group. Southwest has eight total boarding groups, so while there are several ahead of Group 5, it’s better than boarding last.

Each year on your Southwest Plus Card cardmember anniversary, you’ll get a 10% promo code that applies to Southwest flights. Just note that this discount excludes Basic fares.

On your Southwest Plus Card cardmember anniversary every year, you’ll receive 3,000 bonus points. Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and you’ll typically need 83 Rapid Rewards points for every dollar of airfare you book. In other words, those 3,000 Rapid Rewards points should get you around $36 worth of airfare on Southwest annually.

As part of an overhaul of the Rapid Rewards program, Southwest is simplifying TQP earning on credit cards. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on a co-branded Southwest credit card will earn you one TQP. In other words, $35K in spending would earn you Silver, $65K in spending would earn you Gold, and $140K in spending would earn you Platinum.

This earning rate is the same across cards, so this isn’t specific to the Southwest Plus Card.

The Southwest Plus Card offers 25% savings on inflight purchases of Wi-Fi and drinks. Simply pay with your card, and you’ll automatically receive a statement credit for that amount.

The Southwest Plus Card offers a variety of travel & purchase protection benefits, including:

You’ll want to check the cardmember agreement for the full terms & conditions associated with these benefits.

One of the great features of Chase cards is access to Chase Offers, which provides savings on purchases with all kinds of retailers. This program has saved me a significant amount of money.

The Southwest Plus Card is a solid entry-level airline credit card. If you want a credit card from Southwest and want an annual fee as low as possible, then this card could make sense to you.

You’ll receive a 3,000-point bonus on your cardmember anniversary every year, and 25% savings on inflight purchases. The free checked bag benefit can save you $90 on a roundtrip and the complimentary standard seat selection benefit can add up quickly after a few flights. These perks can more than justify the annual fee, and that’s not even accounting for the massive welcome bonus.

However, there are other options that I think can make more sense.

If your main reason for considering the Southwest Rapid Rewards Plus Card is to earn points for Southwest award flights, you might be better off skipping a Southwest co-branded credit card altogether and just earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points. You can transfer Chase points to Southwest to book flights, and cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) have stronger earning categories and benefits overall.

You can also redeem Ultimate Rewards points with other travel partners, not just Southwest, so this option gives you more flexibility.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card (learn more) is one step up from the Southwest Plus Card, with a $149 annual fee. Here’s a look at its key perks:

There’s also the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card (learn more), the most premium personal Southwest card with a $229 annual fee. If you want as many Southwest perks as possible, this is a better pick.

The Southwest Priority Card’s main perks include:

So you’re getting a higher return of 4.8% on Southwest spending on the Priority Card, based on my valuations, and better complimentary seat selection and upgrade options.

If you want a Southwest Rapid Rewards business credit card in place of or in addition to a personal card, I highly recommend considering the Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more). The Southwest Performance Business Card offers the following benefits, which make it the best Southwest credit card, in my opinion:

The Southwest Performance Business Card offers a lot of points, and more perks overall than other Southwest cards.

The Southwest Plus Card is a good entry-level credit card for someone who wants to earn Rapid Rewards points without paying a high annual fee. It’s not the most valuable Southwest credit card in the lineup, but its benefits and strong welcome bonus make it a good option at this price point.

#6075. Allegiant Air Ditches 26 Nonstop Routes: See Full List Now

It is critically important for an airline to know exactly what it is and isn't. The ultra-low-cost carrier, Allegiant Air, knows the answer immediately. It is and always will be unashamedly a leisure-focused operator, with the acquisition of Sun Country by the Allegiant Travel Company strengthening its position.

If Allegiant's network in Q1 2026 (January to March) is compared to what's available in the same three months in 2027, 26 routes have been removed. Inevitably, some of them involve airports to which the airline no longer flies. Mostly, however, the links have simply been removed from still-served airports.

Schedule analysis using OAG data shows that all of the following markets saw the ULCC in Q1 2026 but will not do so in Q1 2027. Some may have had flights in January, February, and March this year, while others may have only had service in one or two of the months.

20 of them have been removed entirely from Allegiant's map due to what is normal route churn. No flights are planned beyond the stated month. The remaining six markets are very different. While they won't be served in the first three months of the new year, they'll simply return later in 2027. Some may say that including them is unfair, but they feature because two different time periods were compared.

Routes (All Served In Q1 2026 But Not In Q1 2027)

Bellingham to Los Angeles, Cincinnati to Los Angeles, Nashville to Peoria, Las Vegas to Boise

Fort Lauderdale to Traverse City, Orlando Sanford to Columbia

Bellingham to Palm Springs, Bellingham to Oakland, Fort Lauderdale to Columbia, Fort Lauderdale to Savannah, Fort Lauderdale to Tri-State/Huntington, Las Vegas to Chattanooga, Pittsburgh to Phoenix Sky Harbor, Punta Gorda to New Orleans

Bellingham to Burbank, Las Vegas to Lexington, Nashville to Akron/Canton, Nashville to Sarasota (returns later in 2027), Portland to Idaho Falls, Washington Dulles to Savannah

Akron/Canton to Myrtle Beach (returns later in 2027), Boston to Des Moines (returns later in 2027), Denver to Knoxville (returns later in 2027), Denver to Peoria (returns later in 2027), Las Vegas to Asheville, Nashville to Gulf Shores (returns later in 2027)

As Allegiant has pulled out of Columbia, Los Angeles International, Oakland, and Palm Springs, the quartet's last remaining routes in the examined period inevitably featured. Los Angeles International joined the carrier's network in 2009. In the past ten years alone, over 13,000 departures were available. It was the carrier's 18th most-served airport in this period.

While the following links were served by Allegiant in the first three months of 2026, they will not have nonstop operations in the same quarter next year. They are not cut, as they'll all return in spring 2027. Most have simply become seasonal, which is, of course, designed to better align capacity with demand to improve yield and load factor performance.

Only 2 departures in January (they all count!), as an extension of winter operations until that month

15 departures in January, February, and March

8 departures in March, when the season resumed

Only 2 departures in January, as an extension of winter operations until that month

Only 1 departure in January, as an extension of winter operations until that month

8 departures in March, when the season resumed

Located in Alabama, not far from Mobile and Pensacola, Gulf Shores welcomed scheduled services a year and a half ago. Allegiant is currently the only operator there, although Sun Country will debut next year. The pair plan 14 routes in 2027, including Nashville.

The route from Tennessee had been on Allegiant's map since November 2025. Between then and August 2026, the load factor was a ridiculously low 64.7%. January and February were among the worst months, which is why flights do not resume until April. If things don't pick up, the route won't be coming back in 2028.

One of the two new routes seems to be doing particularly badly, with big changes coming. Find out more here!

At 1,585 nautical miles (2,935 km) each way, Allegiant had service between Las Vegas and Asheville from March 2021 until November 2026. Not surprisingly, it had two weekly flights, with both the 156-seat A319 and 186-seat A320 deployed. As is often the case, the market did not have nonstop flights until Allegiant's arrival.

DOT data currently extends to August 2026. Between March 2021 and that summer month, Allegiant transported 162,157 round-trip passengers. It had 69% of the local market in this period, with the rest of the traffic flying via hubs with other operators. Allegiant filled 81.2% of the available seats, although the fares needed to achieve that result are unknown.

#6074. FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, said they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

“Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”

Thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

Cruz said at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”

“Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz said. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”

Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

“The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they said.

They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer said they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about plans for such an inquiry.

Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

“As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter said.

On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

“While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

“I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján said, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”

Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., said at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”

“I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that issue,” Moran said.

Moran also said he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.

#6073. Delta Is My Preferred Airline Of The “Big Three” US Carriers (Hear Me Out)

I’ve never been one to take the easy road, so I thought I’d bite the bullet and talk about my love for Delta in what you might call a baptism of fire. Before I jump in, I’m not here screaming that Delta is the best US airline. Far from it. Rather, I’m explaining why, as someone who is not based in the US, Delta is my go-to airline.

This year, Delta has nudged up to fourth most-flown of the 94 airlines I’ve tried out over the years, and I’d like to share a little bit about why.

Starting from the ground, I am a big fan of what Delta is doing with its lounges. Stepping inside one of Delta’s newer Sky Clubs, you feel like you’re in the lobby bar of a luxury hotel rather than the corporate canteen-style spaces offered by competitors.

I know these newer lounges aren’t in every airport yet — Honolulu (HNL) is a notable exception — but lately I’ve found myself enjoying them before the majority of my latest Delta flights departing from a US airport.

Don’t get me started on the Delta One Lounges: I’ve visited locations at LAX and JFK, and these are without a doubt my favorite airline lounges in the US.

Stepping onboard, I actually like the planes. In recent times, I’ve flown mainly on its Airbus A320 family aircraft, a few Boeing 757s (which I love), and once on a Boeing 767-300 from Honolulu to LAX.

I like how they’ve all had seatback screens, I’ve never had an issue using my SkyMiles account to access the fast free WiFi (it’s decent, even though it’s not Starlink), and I’ve never felt uncomfortable on one of Delta’s planes.

I also have to say, I’ve always had pleasant, if not better-than-your-average service when flying Delta.

I love a good redemption as much as the next frequent flyer. However, our credit cards in the UK earn us far fewer points than those in the US, so for me, redeeming points is the exception, not the norm.

As such, I don’t hate on Delta’s SkyMiles for its mostly sky-high redemption rates. Even if finding a one-way in Delta One from Rio or São Paulo to New York for less than 470,000 miles is almost impossible.

Besides, I credit my Delta flights to my Flying Blue account, which is therefore home to my SkyTeam elite status and miles earned on Delta and all other SkyTeam airlines.

Neither do I fly often enough nor have the funds to unlock top-tier status in all three alliances. Aside from the Virgin Atlantic Gold status I got from a status match and my BA Silver, which expires in April, Flying Blue is the only program whose status I’m actively chasing.

As a direct result of Air France and KLM’s membership in the SkyTeam alliance, I actively choose to fly other SkyTeam airlines, such as Delta. Also, thanks to the relationship between Delta and fellow SkyTeam member Aeroméxico, I’ve managed to find great-value cash fares on several occasions when planning travel between Mexico and Canada or the US.

I actually used to be a die-hard American boy until the BA Club was sabotaged. In terms of lounges, aircraft comfort, complimentary amenities (like seat back screens and Wi-Fi), and service, Delta has felt like an upgrade.

For what it’s worth, if status had nothing to do with it, I’d still choose Delta.

My experience with American, Delta, and United has mainly been on domestic flights around the US, including transcons. In fact, I’ve never flown Delta One, American Flagship, or United Polaris on long-haul international flights. Who knows, my top three could reshuffle once I’ve tried and tested each of those. Maybe I’ll have to have a word with Ben about this…

I know Delta gets a bad rep, but honestly I have only had pleasant experiences when flying the airline over the years. As long as I’m being loyal to SkyTeam, it will remain my preference when traveling to or around the US (unless it’s from the UK; then I’m team Virgin).

I’m going to make it a priority to fly each of American, Delta, and United’s best international long-haul products over the coming months. Watch this space for my thoughts on flying those for the first time, and to see whether Delta remains my US number one.

I’m curious, what do you love or hate about Delta?

Airports fill up with travelers, Thanksgiving meals get prepped.

But for flyers hoping to do some cooking before their flight, there are important rules to know.

The Transportation Security Administration's 3-1-1 liquids policy is still in place.

And, yes: It applies to some of the top items you may be thinking of bringing along on your trip, from the cranberry sauce to the jar of gravy.

“It’s weird, but sometimes we will see turkeys at security checkpoints,” former TSA spokesperson Mark Howell once told me.

That means extra work for TSA officers, who already have to contend with one of the busiest weeks of the year at airports.

Last year, the Sunday after Thanksgiving set the record as the busiest day ever at U.S. airports.

If you’re among the travelers hoping to do a little meal prep at home before flying, there are some things you need to know — whether you’ll be waiting in the standard line (arrive early, if so) or heading to the TSA PreCheck line.

Read more: Is air travel ready for Thanksgiving? The meltdown is over, but worries persist

As always, the TSA’s 3-1-1 rule governs what can and can’t come through security.

If what you're packing doesn't meet that criteria, it needs to go in a checked bag if you want to fly with it.

Most travelers know they can’t bring a huge bottle of sunscreen in their carry-on luggage. However, things get a bit more confusing when we start talking Thanksgiving entrees and side dishes.

Related: When will the TSA's 3-1-1 liquids policy end?

Let’s start with the obvious here: You have to follow the 3-1-1 rule whether you’re bringing on a mini bottle of toothpaste or your family’s famous Thanksgiving side dish.

That means you’re good to bring a turkey, ham, chicken or something similar. Just keep in mind that the U.S. Department of Agriculture advises that you give special attention to packing and storing perishables — no one wants to eat a dish that spoiled during your flight.

You can keep your food cool with ice packs, but they must stay frozen through the checkpoint.

If you're bringing a frozen turkey, that also must be frozen when you pass through security. Your best bet: Leave it in the freezer until the moment you leave for the airport.

Other safe bets: You're generally clear to bring stuffing, macaroni and cheese, casseroles, pies, pastries, and fresh fruits and vegetables through the checkpoint. Just be aware they may get a second look or a second trip through the X-ray machine.

With many other classic holiday dishes, you’ll want to consider the ingredients before you try to carry them on. In some cases, it’s a pretty obvious “no-go.”

TSA officers have historically said that if you can "pump it, pour it, spray it or spread it," it needs to be checked — if it's more than 3.4 ounces.

Luckily, if you’re unsure what food can come on the plane, there are a few ways to confirm before your trip.

If your item falls into the “no” category for a carry-on bag, you should still be able to pack it in your checked luggage. This is a good time to use those free checked bags and other airline credits available on that travel credit card in your wallet.

Every time the TSA catches a prohibited item while scanning a bag, it causes a delay at the checkpoint. During what’s expected to be one of the busiest weeks of the year, those delays can add up.

Whether you plan to pack a bottle of hair gel or your family’s traditional Thanksgiving casserole, consider whether the size and composition of your item make it eligible to pass through security.

On the bright side, travelers no longer have to take off their shoes when passing through security.

#6071. When To Use The Flight Attendant Call Button (And When To Skip It)

To push the flight attendant call button, or not to push the flight attendant call button, that is the question. I’ll share my take, and then I’m curious to hear how OMAAT readers feel. Let’s start with some background, and then we’ll discuss best practices…

Every airplane seat has a flight attendant call button, typically in the overhead console, right by the reading light and individual air nozzle (if the plane has those). The flight attendant call button, is, as the name suggests, a way to call a flight attendant to your seat.

The flight attendant call button typically depicts a person with a tray, suggesting that the call button is intended for service. However, that’s not how all flight attendants interpret it, so I want to talk about that in a bit more detail.

In most of the world, the flight attendant call button seems to work as intended. It’s a useful way to call over a flight attendant, whether you want a drink refill, or there’s some sort of an emergency.

However, in the United States I’ve heard several flight attendants over the years announce that the call button is in fact the “emergency flight attendant call button,” advising passengers to only use it if absolutely necessary. Suffice to say that this kind of announcement isn’t approved by any airline.

While people will often joke “well I’m happy you consider my drink request to be an emergency,” let’s talk about when it’s actually appropriate to use a flight attendant call button.

Broadly speaking, it’s always appropriate to use the flight attendant call button for service in first & business class, especially on international airlines. You’re paying a premium for more service, and having an extra request on a long haul flight isn’t unreasonable.

I’ll take it a step further — at top airlines, crews generally prefer that you push the call button rather than going to the galley with your request. Foreign carriers typically have thick curtains between the galley and the cabin, and you generally shouldn’t try to go into the flight attendant’s “space” without permission. They’d much rather come to you. They might be putting on some makeup or eating a meal, and don’t want to be caught off guard. So absolutely push the flight attendant call button — it’s the courteous thing to do.

I do want to mention just one caveat — try to be respectful of the overall service flow. For example, if a cabin has 50+ business class seats and the crew is doing service with a cart and is currently in the aisle, wait until they finish that round of service before pushing the call button again, unless there’s something you absolutely need.

When it comes to using the call button, you can’t beat Emirates first class, where you can voice or video call the crew with any requests, without them even having to come to your seat.

It’s also interesting to observe the cultural differences between airlines when it comes to service approaches. For example, in Singapore Airlines first class I generally don’t push the flight attendant call button, since even on a long haul flight, a crew member seems to pass through the cabin every 10-15 minutes throughout the flight. The service is just so proactive that I don’t find it necessary.

Of course those are both airlines known for great service. You have all kinds of other airlines where flight attendants make a habit of not passing through the cabin, and when they do they almost seem to look down, to avoid making eye contact.

Using the flight attendant call button in economy is trickier. There’s nothing inherently wrong with it, but the staffing ratio in economy is different than in first & business class, and in many cases flight attendants have to walk a lot further to your seat. Also keep in mind that on long haul flights the crew has rest periods, reducing the staffing ratio even further.

Personally I think there’s nothing wrong with using the call button in economy:

That being said, in economy I also think it’s more reasonable to stretch your legs and go to the galley yourself. Generally there’s a small setup with snacks and drinks, at least on long haul flights, so you can help yourself to that. Furthermore, in my experience flight attendants are typically “sitting in the open” more in economy than in business or first class, given that the volume of requests is greater.

The above are my general thoughts, though is the story any different on airlines in the United States? This accounts for the fact that:

On US airlines I’m generally a little more hesitant to use the call button. I see what kind of a vibe the crew gives me. In general I don’t mind pushing the call button in international first & business class on a US airline, while I avoid it on domestic flights. If I get the sense that the crew takes issue with use of the call button, I of course won’t use it.

All airplane seats have individual flight attendant call buttons, though customs around using them seem to differ. In the United States, some flight attendants seem to think these buttons are just for emergencies, while outside the United States there are consistently no issues with using them for service.

Where do you stand on using the flight attendant call button, and what has your experience been?

Us airline here . I’m more than happy to take call lights in any cabin. When it gets concerning is when I customs keeps pressing it for alcohol refills . I have never heard crew members making an announcement that the call light is for emergency only , except when customer press it during taxi, take off , and landing.

Who else ran to the comments to see how you crazy folk use the call button.

I use it in business class if I'm done with a meal and am burried in the set table with plates and all. Without the call button the crew may not proactively come clear it for hours.

If the airline offered complementary drinks, then no reason not to use it to ask for another. Just because they served you one doesn’t make a difference, there’s no cap on how many drinks are complementary so it’s part of the job. If the tray hasn’t been cleared and you need the bathroom. Yes you should feel comfortable calling the crew. If you want your meal early, that’s pushing it. You want an extra blanket? Maybe. You want to adjust the cabin temperature; I’d reserve this request for premium cabins, unless the temperature is ridiculous. Merely my opinion though, of course, now how it practically works - you will always get some cabin crew who don’t want to do extra work so even resent basic aspects of their job like serving drinks or clearing a table so you can, you know, get out of your seat to the bathroom - not really optional! I’m too hot/cold, I can’t wait to eat? Well that’s getting ridiculous. Even as a frequent F traveller I don’t expect them to rush a fine meal service just because I’m impatient. I can see how this will play out totally differently in a cabin with 100 other passengers in close proximity.

I do not care what cabin I’m travelling in, I’m pressing the button if I want something.

Air Canada is the third-largest international operator in North America. In 2026, Cirium Diio data shows that the Star Alliance member has a total of 96,859 international departures. There are an average of 265 daily departures, varying from as few as 214 to as many as 293.

International flights are down by 19% compared to the record set in 2018. This is driven by the US market, which is at the 18th-lowest level in the past 20 years, partly due to the political situation. However, even long-haul activity is down. The overall picture is less bleak for international seats for sale, as Air Canada is using higher-capacity equipment, with a record of 171 seats per flight.

The Canadian carrier's long-haul network from January 2026 through January 2027 was compared to what is scheduled for February 2027 onwards. This process identified that the following two long-haul routes have been pulled or will end soon. Both have been revealed before, with this article simply summarizing what is happening.

This route only existed for one season, with 35 departures. The market had not previously had any nonstop flights. The 737 MAX 8 was used

Route served since 2024. See below the table. The 787-9 is deployed

The upcoming cessation of flights to Singapore was probably influenced by the high price of fuel, which necessarily means that the economics of ultra-long-haul routes worsens. Intriguingly, Delta Air Lines looks set to announce a new route from Seattle to Asia next week, which will seemingly be to Singapore. It'll be betting on the price of fuel reducing meaningfully before its first flight lifts off.

Canada's flag carrier flew to Lion City for years until 1991. When service resumed 33 years later in April 2024, flights were nonstop for the first time. Air Canada's return was because of the exit of Singapore Airlines, whose final departure from British Columbia was in September 2023. The Asian carrier's flights were often tagged with those to Seattle, with that route continuing on a nonstop standalone basis today.

Air Canada's exit will come less than three years after the Vancouver route was launched. Covering a considerable 6,923 nautical miles (12,821 km) each way on a great circle basis, the airline runs five times weekly on the 787-9. It is currently the airline's longest nonstop service.

Codesharing with Singapore Airlines was important, with approximately 35% of the market transferring in Changi.

One of the two new routes seems to be doing particularly badly, with big changes coming. Find out more here!

As you'll know by now, Air Canada has entirely pulled out of New York JFK. Airport churn is not uncommon, and all airlines do it. The Canadian carrier has also fully exited from Charleston, with its existence at the coastal city in South Carolina lasting for two-and-a-half years.

The route began in March 2023. Air Canada continues to operate between Montreal and Newark and LaGuardia. However, no airline now serves flies between Montreal and JFK

#6069. Sanders: ‘Medicare for All’ will be HELP priority

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders said Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care plan if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

Democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

Sanders said Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

His version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

“If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders said, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion plan, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

While who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of New York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders said he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”

Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”

In addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said last week that he plans to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”

Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee issues, he looks forward to finding common ground.

#6068. Buy IHG One Rewards Points With 100% Bonus (0.5 Cents Each): Worth It?

IHG One Rewards is currently offering a limited time 100% bonus on purchased points. With this, IHG One Rewards members can purchase points for as little as 0.5 cents each. Is this a good deal?

While I wouldn’t recommend buying points without a specific use in mind, there are absolutely ways to get outsized value, and this is in line with the best offers that we see from the program. With the right strategy, this could be an opportunity to get a significant discount on an IHG hotel stay, and I’ll show exactly how.

Link: Buy IHG One Rewards points with this promotion with a 100% bonus

Here’s every promotion on purchased IHG Rewards Points we’ve tracked since January 2026, with the cost per point for each, so you can see how the current deal stacks up.

Is this a good deal? At 0.54 cents per point, the current promotion is 50% below the standard price. That matches the best deal we’ve tracked.

Cost per point at the largest purchase tier, including the 7.5% tax. Lower is better.

Every IHG Rewards Club buy points promotion since January 2026

*Cost per point is for the largest purchase tier and includes the 7.5% tax.

Between 12:01 AM ET on November 23 and 11:59PM ET on December 11, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a bonus on purchased points. Points can be purchased in increments of 1,000 points, and the bonus is structured as follows:

Note that the purchase of IHG points doesn’t count toward elite status, and purchased points will post within 72 hours of an eligible purchase (though usually much faster than that). Furthermore, the purchase of points is non-refundable.

Ordinarily you can buy IHG One Rewards points for as little as one cent each (the pricing isn’t linear), before any discounts or bonuses, and that’s inclusive of all taxes and fees.

With that in mind, if you were eligible for a 100% bonus and purchased 300,000 IHG One Rewards points pre-bonus, you’d receive a total of 600,000 points at a cost of $3,000, which is a rate of 0.5 cents per IHG point.

While The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), offer a 30% discount on purchased points, that benefit only applies when buying points at the normal cost, and wouldn’t be applicable here.

IHG One Rewards ordinarily lets members purchase up to 150,000 points per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion that cap has been increased to 300,000 points, pre-bonus.

IHG One Rewards points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you pay with an IHG credit card, you wouldn’t earn any bonus rewards, so it’s not treated as if it’s IHG spending.

Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

IHG One Rewards has dynamic award pricing, which means there’s no minimum or maximum number of points a hotel stay can cost. Rather, the cost of an award stay generally correlates somewhat to the cost of a revenue stay.

However, that doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll get the same value with all hotel stays. There are many situations where you can get outsized value by buying points and then redeeming them. Let me just give a few examples, using stays I pulled up for random dates (again, pricing is dynamic, so this won’t reflect what you see every day).

For example, the Six Senses Kyoto is bookable for 165,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $825.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $1,493.

On the other end of the spectrum, the Holiday Inn Express & Suites Tampa is bookable for 33,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $165.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $230.

However, this won’t always be a good deal. For example, take the Kimpton Tres Rios in Playa del Carmen is bookable for 104,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $520.

That’s not a good deal compared to the cash cost, which is $429, so there you’d be better off just paying cash directly.

Another thing to keep in mind is that select IHG co-branded credit cards offer free night awards, and those are worth up to a certain number of points. What’s great is that these free night awards can typically be topped off with points, so there could be merit to buying IHG points so that you have points with which to top off these certificates.

You’ll get the most value from your IHG points if you have The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more).

That’s because the cards offer a fourth night free benefit, meaning that you can book a four night award stay for the cost of three nights. This is essentially the equivalent of 25% off in increments of four nights, since you can use this benefit an unlimited number of times.

Just to use the Six Senses Kyoto example above, if you earned 495,000 points (worth $2,475 at 0.5 cents per point), that would be enough for four nights with the fourth night free. That represents an absolutely massive discount.

IHG has over 15 hotel brands, so there are lots of options for redeeming your IHG One Rewards points. IHG points can be redeemed at the following properties, among others:

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider IHG points to be worth 0.5 cents each, and I tend to value points pretty conservatively. So the purchase price is around what I value these points.

For non-elite members, IHG One Rewards points expire after 12 months of inactivity. However, any sort of points earning or redemption activity would reset the expiration of your points. Furthermore, IHG One Rewards points don’t expire for elite members in the program.

Keep in mind that IHG elite status is quite easy to earn. Just for having The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more) or The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), you receive Platinum status, without any sort of a spending requirement.

IHG One Rewards doesn’t have blackout dates on award nights, but the program does have capacity controls. What this means is that some number of standard rooms will be made available for award redemptions every night, but that doesn’t mean that all standard rooms are available for award redemptions.

IHG One Rewards is offering a sale on purchased points. Through December 11, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a promotion, and members seem to be eligible for a 100% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for 0.5 cents each.

There are instances where buying points can save you over 50% on the cost of a luxury hotel stay. I also think there’s value in having a “reserve” of IHG points, given the brand’s global footprint. You can get even more value out of buying IHG points in conjunction with a premium IHG credit card, so you can get a fourth night free on award redemptions.

Do you plan on buying IHG points with a bonus?
